cards.explanation: The answer is that wisdom brightens his face. The Teacher says a man's wisdom brightens his face, and the sternness of his face is changed. Wisdom works like a warm oven on a cold morning, because it warms up the whole look of a person. Wise folks tend to look like they just remembered where they left the good cookies, friends.

The answer is because of your oath before God. The Teacher says, “Keep the king’s command, I say, because of your oath before God.” So this is about a promise made before God. A promise like that is worth keeping, friends, even when keeping it is a pain.

The answer is that he will do whatever he pleases. The Teacher says not to persist in a bad cause, “…for he will do whatever he pleases.” When one person holds the crown, pushing and pushing in front of him is a risky move. Wise folks know when to stop talking, friends, and I say that as someone with a mustache that never stops.

The answer is False. The Teacher says the king's word is supreme and asks who can say to him, what are you doing. Nobody gets to walk up and question the crown. When the king does whatever he pleases, that question is a big one to ask.
The answer is True. The Teacher says, “Whoever keeps his command will come to no harm…” That's a calm promise for anyone standing before a king. Keeping the command is the safe road, friends.

The answer is the right time and procedure. The Teacher says a wise heart “…knows the right time and procedure.” It's knowing when and how, not only what. A good heart reads the clock and the recipe both.

The answer is False. The Teacher says no one knows what will happen, and asks who can tell him what is to come. Even after talking about right timing, he reminds us that the future is out of our sight. A wise heart knows the time to act, but it can't see around the corner.

The answer is his day of death. The Teacher says, “…so no one has authority over his day of death.” A man can't hold back the wind, and he can't hold back that day either. It's a serious thing, so I'll just say it plainly and let it sit.

The answer is False. The Teacher says that as no one can be discharged in wartime, “…so wickedness will not release those who practice it.” The verse doesn't say they can walk away any time they like. It says wickedness won't release them. It's a hard line, so I won't joke on it.

The answer is that they are praised. The Teacher says the wicked who used to go in and out of the holy place “…were praised in the city where they had done so.” Then he says, “This too is futile.” I think that scene bothered him, friends.

The answer is that they become fully set on doing evil. The Teacher says, “When the sentence for a crime is not speedily executed, the hearts of men become fully set on doing evil.” A slow answer to a wrong turn sends hearts further down it. It's a sobering thing to say, so I'll leave it plain.

The answer is fear. The Teacher says, “…it will go well with those who fear God, who are reverent in His presence.” He says it right after noticing a sinner can do evil a hundred times and still live long. Still, he says he knows it. That's a steady word in a confusing stretch.

The answer is False. The Teacher says that because the wicked do not fear God, “…it will not go well with them, and their days will not lengthen like a shadow.” Their days don't stretch out the way an evening shadow does. It's a firm word after a very confusing stretch, friends.

The answer is that they get what the wicked deserve. The Teacher says, “There are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve…” Then he says, “I say that this too is futile.” That one sends the eyebrows up, and I think it sent his up too.

The answer is True. The Teacher says, “…and there are wicked men who get what the actions of the righteous deserve.” It's the same verse flipped around, like somebody swapped the labels on the cookie boxes. Some righteous men get what the wicked deserve, and some wicked men get what the righteous deserve. He says plainly that this too is futile.

The answer is the enjoyment of life. The Teacher says, “So I commended the enjoyment of life…” Then he adds that nothing is better under the sun than to eat and drink and be merry. After all that puzzling, he lands on gladness, and I like his landing, friends.

The answer is God. The Teacher says this joy will go with a man “…during the days of his life that God gives him under the sun.” So the days are a gift from God, and the joy comes along on them. It's a kind thought.

The answer is that he is unable to comprehend it. The Teacher says he saw every work of God, and that a man is unable to comprehend the work that is done under the sun. He goes on, “Despite his efforts to search it out, he cannot find its meaning…” A man can work and work, and the whole picture stays out of reach. Honest and humble, and I like it, friends.
The answer is False. The Teacher says, “even if the wise man claims to know, he is unable to comprehend.” A claim isn't the same as comprehending. Even the wise man falls short of it, friends.
